# Pilot — legislation.gov.uk

**Real data.** Generated by `tools/adapters/legislation-uk.py` from the UK statute book,
which publishes CLML, Akoma Ntoso, and ELI-style identifiers.

```bash
python3 tools/adapters/legislation-uk.py --uri ukpga/2014/30 \
  --out examples/pilot-uk-legislation
```

Taxation of Pensions Act 2014: 11 parts, 122 sections, 136 entities.

`code` makes the strongest architectural claims in schemaGov — that schema.org's
ELI-derived vocabulary does nearly all the work, that the FRBR work/expression split is real
rather than theoretical, and that document structure belongs to Akoma Ntoso rather than here.
This is the test of those claims.

## The FRBR claim is confirmed, in the source's own words

legislation.gov.uk's Akoma Ntoso rendering carries FRBR identification explicitly:

```
FRBRWork           http://www.legislation.gov.uk/id/ukpga/2014/30    enacted    2014-12-17
FRBRExpression     .../ukpga/2014/30/2016-09-15                      validFrom  2016-09-15
FRBRManifestation  .../2016-09-15/data.akn                           transform
```

That is precisely the three levels the profile encodes — `Legislation` as the work,
`legislationDateVersion` as the expression, `LegislationObject` as the manifestation. The
profile was built from the ELI specification without ever seeing a statute book, and a real
national statute book publishes the same structure.

The Work URI is also exactly what the adapter had independently chosen as `@id`, which is
useful confirmation that the identity model matches practice rather than merely being
defensible.

## The defect it found

**`legislationDateVersion` was being read from the wrong field.**

The adapter first took it from `dc:modified` — 2017-02-07. The FRBR Expression date is
**2016-09-15**. Those are different things: `dc:modified` is when the *record* was last
touched; the Expression date is what the *consolidated text is valid at*. Nearly eighteen
months apart on this act.

`legislationDateVersion` is defined as "the point-in-time at which the provided description of
the legislation is valid", so the Expression date is correct and the modification date is
simply a different fact. Getting this wrong means citing a consolidation as current when it is
not — the exact failure the field exists to prevent. The adapter now reads FRBR from the AKN.

## Structure is linked, not absorbed

The act is published in three renderings, and the profile carries all three with their legal
value distinguished:

| Format | Legal value |
|---|---|
| `application/akn+xml` (Akoma Ntoso) | Official |
| `application/xml` (CLML) | Official |
| `text/html` | Unofficial |

The profile stores the Part/Section hierarchy as `Legislation` entities linked by
`isPartOf`/`hasPart` with `codificationLevel`, and stops there. Clause-level markup —
provisos, definitions, amendment instructions — stays in the AKN, linked through `encoding`
and `conformsTo`. That is [SPEC §1.4](../../SPEC.md) working exactly as written, against a
publisher that produces both.

## What remains untested

**The amendment graph.** The profile's most distinctive claim is that ELI's six relations —
`legislationAmends`, `legislationRepeals`, `legislationChanges`, `legislationConsolidates`,
`legislationCorrects`, `legislationCommences` — replace a single blunt `supersedes`.

This act's AKN carries **no** `textualMod` elements, and the `/changes/affected/` endpoint
returns HTML rather than machine-readable data despite a 200. So the amendment relations are
still unexercised against real data. Ironically the act is itself heavily amending — its
section titles read *"In section 165(1) of FA 2004 (the pension rules)..."* — but those
amendments are expressed as prose in the text, not as structured relations in the metadata.

That is worth stating plainly: **the part of the `code` profile most likely to be wrong is
the part no publicly available source has yet been able to test.**
